tldr: A single-policy whole-body locomotion control system was realized, enabling a humanoid to autonomously switch between flat-ground walking and full-body parkour—such as climbing and vaulting—based on context, using only an onboard depth camera and velocity commands.
hero_caption: The overall framework of Light-Loco-Parkour. Locomotion and individual parkour skill teachers are trained separately with reinforcement learning and distilled into a single policy, followed by reward-driven transition learning and distillation to an onboard depth camera before real-world deployment.
overview:
When humanoid robots navigate cluttered real-world environments, walking solely on their legs reaches its limits. Full-body contact motions—such as vaulting by pushing off with hands or hooking a knee to climb, just like humans do—are indispensable. However, existing control systems either merely track predetermined motion trajectories without adapting to terrain changes, or are confined to leg-dominated locomotion, leaving the arms and torso largely unused for overcoming obstacles.

To tackle this, the authors propose "Light-Loco-Parkour (LightLP)". The core idea lies in taking just a single coarse motion seed extracted from video or other sources, self-expanding it within a physics simulator to fit obstacles to acquire diverse contact-rich skills, distilling these multiple skills and perceptive locomotion into a "single neural network", and enabling autonomous transitions driven purely by rewards without external skill-switching commands.

The method was applied to a custom 90 cm tall compact humanoid, "Lightbot 0", and evaluated zero-shot in both simulation and real-world (indoor and outdoor) settings. As a result, the authors demonstrated that tasks ranging from stepping stones, narrow balance beams, and outdoor stairs to hand-supported climbing (climb-and-step), one-handed vaulting (speed-vault), and pelvis-contact turning vaults (reverse-vault) can be executed remarkably well as a single policy on an onboard low-power edge PC (Jetson Orin Nano).
contributions: Constructing an end-to-end pipeline that integrates parkour skills involving whole-body contact with objects into a velocity-tracking perceptive locomotion policy, allowing a single policy to seamlessly handle open-terrain running, obstacle traversal, and locomotion resumption.

Developing a method to self-expand just a single coarse seed motion extracted from video into a set of dynamically feasible, terrain-paired motion references matching obstacle geometry using a physics simulator.

Enabling autonomous acquisition of transitions to appropriate whole-body skills purely from reward based on onboard depth images and velocity commands, without using one-hot skill labels or hand-coded state machines.

sections.heading: Legs alone won't cut it: Taking on whole-body parkour
sections.summary: To traverse rubble and cluttered environments where wheels or tracks cannot pass, whole-body contact leveraging the arms and torso is essential. This section reviews the challenges faced by conventional motion imitation and RL-based locomotion, explaining the goals and contributions of the single-policy whole-body perceptive locomotion system "LightLP" designed to overcome them.
sections.details:
For humanoids to truly operate in human-like environments, whole-body motions—not just stepping with legs, but pressing on handrails with hands or hooking knees—are necessary. However, prior research approaches have had distinct trade-offs.

The first approach, "Motion Imitation", traces movements from motion capture or video to produce dynamic motions, but tends to fail when encountering terrain absent from the training data. Furthermore, motion data involving obstacle contact is extremely scarce.
The second approach, "Locomotion via Reinforcement Learning", can acquire robust walking that tracks velocity commands and adapts to rough terrain. However, leaving behavior solely to reward maximization inevitably leads to relying only on the legs, rarely discovering contact-rich skills like climbing or vaulting that make full use of the arms and torso.

Achieving whole-body perceptive locomotion that unifies these requires overcoming three major hurdles:
- Data scarcity: Motion data where hands and feet accurately contact obstacles and remain physically feasible within robot torque limits is exceedingly rare.
- Skill generalization: Rather than simply replaying reference motions, the robot must adapt contact timing appropriately even when obstacle height and width vary.
- Autonomous skill transitions: Smoothly switching from walking to vaulting and from vaulting back to walking based solely on vision and velocity commands, without external instructions.

LightLP realizes a system where a single policy assesses situations and acts using only onboard depth camera footage and velocity commands by self-expanding coarse seed motions in a physics simulator to generate high-quality reference data, combined with teacher-student distillation and transition learning.

sections.heading: At the crossroads of locomotion control and motion imitation
sections.summary: This section surveys the evolution of perceptive locomotion from model predictive control to recent deep reinforcement learning, along with the history of whole-body skill imitation using video and mocap data. It clarifies where this research sets itself apart from the computational burden and unnatural motions of existing whole-body parkour methods.
sections.details:
Related work broadly divides into two lineages: perceptive locomotion control and humanoid motion imitation.

In perceptive locomotion, approaches include explicitly building elevation maps using LiDAR or similar sensors to plan footholds, and end-to-end methods that feed raw depth camera images directly into the policy. The former risks missteps during map drift, and recently the effectiveness of end-to-end methods has been demonstrated in quadrupeds and bipeds. However, prior humanoid studies overcoming obstacles with the whole body (such as PHP and MGMT) suffer from limitations: they rely on manually generated offline reference trajectories causing the robot to be magnetically drawn toward obstacles, or require additional computers to run heavy diffusion models during inference.

On the other hand, in humanoid motion imitation, methods tracking reference trajectories frame-by-frame (such as DeepMimic and BeyondMimic) and methods learning human motion style via generative adversarial networks (like AMP) have advanced. However, these primarily focus on flat-ground movement, making it difficult to handle dense contact with external environments such as handrails and obstacles. While methods exist to recover 3D skeletons from video (like GVHMR), camera parameter errors cause interpenetration with obstacles, leading to physical breakdown.

LightLP overcomes these challenges by introducing self-expansion that uses the physics simulator itself as a retargeting mechanism, alongside a distillation pipeline that resolves to a single lightweight network during inference, enabling natural, low-latency whole-body perceptive locomotion.

sections.heading: System overview: Four modules and the training workflow
sections.summary: This section explains the overall architecture of LightLP. It consists of a four-stage pipeline: training a perceptive locomotion teacher using privileged information, self-expanding seed motions, distilling multi-skills into a single height-scan policy, and re-distilling to an onboard depth camera for real-world deployment.
sections.details:
The training process of LightLP proceeds in orderly steps, as shown in Figure F2.

1. Perceptive Locomotion Learning: A robust teacher policy for traversing diverse rough terrains is trained using privileged height scans (elevation meshes of the surrounding terrain).
2. Skill Acquisition and Expansion: Starting from a single seed motion extracted from video or other sources, the obstacle height is gradually increased while maintaining physical feasibility in the simulator, automatically generating feasible motion data perfectly paired with terrain.
3. Multi-Skill Distillation and Transition Learning: The behaviors of the locomotion teacher and individual skill teachers are integrated into a single height-scan student policy using DAgger (imitation learning where the student mimics teacher actions in student-visited states). Furthermore, reinforcement learning is conducted in a "Transition Group" environment mixing locomotion and skills to acquire autonomous switching behavior.
4. Depth Distillation for Real Hardware: The policy is finally distilled from the clean height scans unique to simulation into a policy that takes noisy, narrow-field-of-view real-world monocular depth camera images as input.

The problem is formulated as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) as the reinforcement learning algorithm. IsaacLab is used as the simulation environment, and on the real robot, it outputs 50 Hz PD target joint positions.

captions.F2: The overall pipeline of LightLP. Showing (a) individual training of perceptive locomotion and skills using privileged information, (b) integration via multi-expert DAgger and reward-driven transition learning, and (c) the final distillation process to onboard depth images.

sections.heading: Teaching foot safety: Reward and architecture design for perceptive locomotion
sections.summary: This section details the training method for the base perceptive locomotion policy. It explains unique techniques such as an asymmetric actor-critic structure to cross demanding footholds like stepping stones and balance beams, virtual foot scans to prevent stepping off edges, and history filters to soften landing impacts.
sections.details:
The success of the perceptive locomotion policy hinges on a reward design that prevents missteps on challenging terrain while avoiding hesitation in moving forward.

- Network Architecture and Asymmetric Actor-Critic:
The actor of the teacher policy takes proprioception from the past 5 frames (joint positions and angular velocities) and clean height scans as input, constructed entirely with MLPs. CNNs were also evaluated, but MLPs were chosen because CNNs merely increased training time without performance differences. An "asymmetric actor-critic" setup is adopted, providing the critic with privileged information not shown to the actor, such as local foot scans and full base velocity. This enhances value estimation accuracy while keeping excessive privileged information that students cannot imitate out of the actor.

- Velocity-Slack Bonus:
On difficult terrain like stepping stones, robots tend to freeze before obstacles out of fear of falling. Because strict velocity-tracking rewards cause forward motion to halt, a slack reward introducing a gentle tolerance band around the command velocity $v_x$ was incorporated. As a result, the robot can decelerate before obstacles to choose footholds carefully without penalty, sustaining forward progress.

- Illegal-Footstep Penalty:
In environments like stepping stones or balance beams, foot placement must not hang off edges. In this method, a downward virtual ray grid is placed on each of the robot's soles (Figure F3), penalizing the proportion of rays that penetrate deeper than $\delta = 0.1$ m during stance.

- Landing Acceleration Penalty:
Excessive acceleration exceeding $30\,\text{m/s}^2$ on the feet is accumulated and penalized using a first-order exponential decay filter with time constant $\tau = 0.06$ s. By penalizing history rather than instantaneous spikes, the robot naturally adopts "anticipatory foot placement," decelerating its foot right before touchdown to land softly.

Terrains form a grid curriculum of 10 difficulty levels—including stairs, slopes, stepping stones, and balance beams (Figure F4)—efficiently trained by promoting or demoting environments according to command velocity tracking.

captions.F3: Diagram of virtual height scans placed under the soles. Rays cast downward from each foot detect the extent to which the foot hangs over edges or hovers over gaps on stepping stones to compute penalties.
captions.F4: Diverse procedural terrains used in locomotion training. Arranged in order of difficulty: (1) slopes, (2) Perlin noise rough terrain, (3) flat ground, (4) rails, (5) pillar clusters, (6) stepping stones, (7) obstacle boxes, (8) stairs, and (9) balance beam bridges.

sections.heading: From a single video to parkour: Self-expansion and label-free autonomous transitions
sections.summary: This section explains the core method for acquiring whole-body parkour skills from a single human video clip, adapting to obstacle sizes, and learning autonomous switching with locomotion. It reveals the self-expansion loop via physics simulation, skill generalization combining DAgger and PPO, and transition learning driven purely by rewards.
sections.details:
This chapter represents the primary technical highlight of LightLP, composed of the following three stages:

- 1. Data Expansion (Self-Expansion Loop):
A human 3D skeleton is extracted from a short video clip (such as from YouTube) via GVHMR and retargeted to the robot. Naturally, hands and feet penetrate obstacles, but here the simulator's physics engine is used as a "retargeting corrector". Global position tracking rewards are assigned to contact bodies like wrists, elbows, and pelvis (Figure F5), training non-penetrating motions under physical constraints. Furthermore, by running an "iterative self-expansion loop" where successful simulation trajectories serve as subsequent reference motions while lifting obstacles and motions by 5–10 cm at each step, a diverse set of physically consistent reference data across various heights is automatically built from a single video.

- 2. Skill Learning and Generalization:
From the generated data, the most demanding expert operating closest to hardware torque and velocity limits is selected and distilled via DAgger into a policy sharing the same observation space as locomotion (height scan + velocity command). Because pure imitation fails to recover in out-of-distribution states, a PPO reinforcement learning loss is simultaneously applied (DAgger + PPO). Subsequently, obstacle positions are randomized and goal-reaching rewards are added, elevating it into a generalized skill that does not overfit to specific locations or shapes.

- 3. Reward-Driven Transition Learning:
The locomotion policy $\pi_p$ and individual skill policies $\{\pi_i\}$ are first distilled into a single student network via multi-expert DAgger. At this stage, the robot can only execute behaviors specific to each environment. Therefore, a "Transition Group" environment mixing flat ground and obstacles is introduced for additional fine-tuning (Figure F6). Without any hand-coded switching rules, only a "conditioned AMP"—which switches the motion style reference from walking AMP (Adversarial Motion Prior) before obstacles to skill AMP past a trigger point—and a sparse goal reward upon reaching behind the obstacle are provided. The robot learns to judge on its own "which skill to trigger now" based on onboard depth and velocity commands.

captions.F5: Designation of body parts where global position tracking rewards are applied (red circles). Configured for (a) the pelvis in reverse-vault, (b) the wrists in climb-and-step, and (c) the elbows in speed-vault.
captions.F6: Structure of the Transition Group environment. The robot is randomly reset across three regions: walking area, skill area, and behind the obstacle; passing the trigger line switches the motion prior (AMP) from walking to skill.

sections.heading: From simulation to the real world: Final distillation to monocular depth
sections.summary: This section describes adapting the policy from wide-angle, complete height scans to the narrow-field, noisy RealSense depth camera on the real robot. Key elements include latent memory via GRU with an auxiliary reconstruction task, and the introduction of noise models mimicking real camera characteristics.
sections.details:
While the height scans used in simulation capture omnidirectional terrain, the real robot only has a single monocular RealSense D435 mounted on the chest angled 30 degrees downward. In particular, during vaulting or climbing, the torso leans forward causing the camera to see only the ground or sky, frequently leading to obstacles disappearing from view (occlusion).

To resolve this, a GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) was integrated into the policy to maintain past frame information as latent memory. Furthermore, during training, an auxiliary reconstruction task (Reconstruction Loss) was introduced to reconstruct the privileged height scan seen by the teacher from the GRU hidden state. This allows the robot to retain terrain information in its mind even when obstacles temporarily leave the camera's view (this decoder is discarded during inference).

Additionally, to bridge the Sim-to-Real gap, the noise characteristics of real cameras were meticulously injected into the simulation:
- Gaussian noise scaled with distance $d$: standard deviation $0.005 + 0.02d$ [m]
- Global depth scale jitter: $\pm 5\%$
- Block-wise dropout: reproducing RealSense-specific invalid regions
- Latency and framerate: simulating 30–60 ms delay and 27–33 Hz framerate fluctuations

Final fine-tuning under these severe conditions ensured zero-shot real-world deployment.

sections.heading: Breaking the 90 cm barrier: Hardware validation and benchmark comparisons
sections.summary: This section reports real-world experiments on the custom 90 cm humanoid "Lightbot 0", along with rigorous comparative evaluations and ablation studies in simulation. The results demonstrate obstacle clearance capabilities far exceeding prior methods, alongside accurate command following.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted using "Lightbot 0" (Figure F7), a custom humanoid measuring 90 cm tall, weighing 18.9 kg, and having 21 degrees of freedom. Actuator torques are 45 N·m for the lower body and 15 N·m for the arms—quite underpowered compared to the 1.3 m class robots used in prior work—yet it exhibited extraordinary athletic capabilities thanks to this method's careful contact planning. Inference runs at 50 Hz on the onboard Jetson Orin Nano.

- Real-World Experimental Results (Figures F8, F9):
The robot smoothly navigated outdoor grass and curbed stairs, as well as indoor balance beams and stepping stones. Furthermore, zero-shot success was achieved for: "speed-vault", sprinting with an approach run up to 3.14 m/s and clearing an obstacle by pushing off with one hand; "reverse-vault", leaping, rotating 360 degrees mid-air, and absorbing impact on the pelvis; and "climb-and-step", scaling a 75 cm platform corresponding to 83% of its body height. It also adapted to unseen trapezoidal obstacles (vaulting boxes) by recognizing their geometry.

- Benchmark Comparisons (Table V):
Comparing the obstacle-to-height ratio $h/H$, while prior works like PHP and MGMT reached around $0.60H$, this method achieved $0.83H$ climbing. On stepping stones and stairs, it also recorded higher success rates than specialized methods (BeamDojo and CReF).

- Ablation Studies (Tables V, VII):
Replacing the GRU with an MLP caused success rates to plummet, confirming the importance of memorizing terrain that has vanished from view. Moreover, removing the Transition Group caused the probability of getting stuck and colliding before obstacles to surge, dropping success rates to 0–33%; adding transition learning boosted this to 98% (t-SNE visualizations in Figure F11 also clearly illustrate mode separation in latent space).

Furthermore, in a test where a backward velocity command was given while facing an obstacle, the robot retreated 100% according to instructions, rather than being drawn toward the obstacle like prior methods. This proves it balances velocity commands and terrain perception rather than being blindly guided by vision alone.

captions.F7: The compact 90 cm humanoid "Lightbot 0" used in experiments. Showing joint torque limits (45 N·m for legs/waist, 15 N·m for arms) and the chest-mounted RealSense depth camera.

sections.heading: Summary and outlook: Toward true all-terrain adaptation
sections.summary: This section synthesizes the achievements of LightLP, confirming the realization of whole-body parkour perceptive locomotion with a single policy. It also presents frank challenges—such as current manual seed alignment and camera field-of-view limits—alongside future directions like active perception.
sections.details:
Light-Loco-Parkour is a breakthrough system that integrates whole-body parkour and perceptive locomotion using only an onboard depth camera and velocity commands, without relying on prior motion trajectories, one-hot skill specifications, or hand-coded state machines. Data self-expansion leveraging the simulator, teacher-student distillation, and reward-driven transition learning underpin this high degree of autonomy.

At the same time, the authors acknowledge several clear limitations:
- Effort in seed generation: Initial alignment between video-extracted motions and virtual obstacles still requires human intervention, presenting a bottleneck to scaling up skill varieties.
- Obstacle density: Currently, isolated obstacles dominate; in extremely cluttered environments where multiple obstacles appear continuously or overlap, transitions can destabilize.
- Fixed chest camera limits: Large arm motions or forward-leaning postures during jumping cause field-of-view blockage, currently relying entirely on GRU memory.

In the future, the authors plan to adapt to more complex environments by introducing "Active Perception"—where the robot actively controls its neck and camera orientation to look where needed—and scaling up motion reference datasets.

takeaways: Obstacle discrepancies arising during retargeting from video can be resolved by using the physics simulator itself as a constrained optimizer (retargeting corrector).

When unifying multiple advanced skills into one policy, a two-stage approach—training separate experts, distilling them via DAgger, and fine-tuning with reinforcement learning in a dedicated Transition Group environment—is exceptionally effective.

When performing whole-body motions with a monocular camera, incorporating recurrent architectures like GRU and imposing an auxiliary task to reconstruct privileged height scans from hidden states effectively counters occlusion.

Meticulous reward engineering balancing contact and forward progress—such as velocity-slack bonuses (tracking rewards with tolerance) and sole virtual-ray penalties—is vital for viable perceptive locomotion.
limitations: Creating seed motions from video still requires manual virtual obstacle alignment, falling short of fully automated large-scale skill generation.
In extreme environments with back-to-back obstacles, transition decisions based on sparse goal rewards become difficult, leading to unstable behavior.
Relying on a fixed monocular depth camera on the chest does not fundamentally eliminate field-of-view occlusion caused by aggressive posture changes or arm intrusions.
